title: India Just Wiped Seven Years of Import Duties on Nuclear Fuel. The Signal Is Bigger Than the Tax Break.
excerpt: A retrospective customs exemption covering imports since 2019 clears legal fog around India's nuclear supply chain — and underlines the urgency of the 100 GW target.
body:
India's finance ministry has waived customs duties on all goods imported for nuclear power generation between April 2019 and January 2026 — a seven-year retrospective exemption that formalises what had been an informal practice and clears the path for the country's ambitious push to expand nuclear capacity to 100 gigawatts by 2047.

The notification, signed by Under Secretary Indrajit Panda and dated June 11, was issued under Section 28A of the Customs Act, 1962. It covers imports of non-irradiated fuel elements and cartridges used in nuclear reactors, effectively eliminating any potential customs liability on shipments made during the covered period.

What Changed

The exemption is not new in principle. India's annual budget in February had already extended customs duty exemptions for nuclear power equipment through 2035. But the finance ministry's latest order applies the benefit backwards — covering nearly seven years of imports that were, in practice, brought in duty-free under an informal understanding but had never been formally exempted.

By issuing the retrospective notification, the government has removed the legal ambiguity that could have exposed importers — principally the Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd. (NPCIL), the state-run monopoly operator of India's civilian reactors — to potential tax demands on past shipments.

The move also shields companies in India's broader nuclear supply chain. Shares of MTAR Technologies, which manufactures precision-engineered components for nuclear reactors and has supplied roughly 70 per cent of the parts for India's prototype fast breeder reactor, jumped 13 per cent on the day of the announcement. Walchandnagar Industries and Power Mech Projects, both linked to nuclear infrastructure, also advanced.

India's Nuclear Ambitions

India currently has 24 operational nuclear reactors with a combined installed capacity of about 8.2 gigawatts — a small fraction of the country's total electricity generation. But the government has set a target of 100 GW of nuclear capacity by 2047, which would require building dozens of new reactors across the country.

The target is part of a broader clean energy strategy that also includes 500 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030. Nuclear power, which operates around the clock regardless of weather, is seen as a critical complement to intermittent solar and wind generation.

Expanding nuclear capacity at the planned pace will require massive imports of fuel assemblies, reactor components, and specialised equipment — imports that the retrospective duty waiver now makes formally cost-free.

The Diaspora Connection

For NRIs tracking India's energy transition, the nuclear customs waiver is part of a pattern. The government has been systematically lowering barriers to nuclear expansion: opening the sector to greater private participation, investing in indigenous reactor designs including the prototype fast breeder reactor at Kalpakkam, and negotiating fuel supply agreements with countries including France, Russia, and the United States.

India's nuclear supply chain is also becoming an investment theme. MTAR Technologies — whose nuclear segment accounts for 26 per cent of its ₹2,582 crore order book — has emerged as a proxy for the sector's growth. Each new reactor represents roughly ₹1,500 crore in revenue opportunity for the company alone.

The retrospective waiver, while technical in nature, sends a signal that the government is serious about removing friction from the nuclear pipeline. For a country that imports the third-largest quantity of oil in the world and has seen its markets battered by the Iran war's impact on crude prices, the urgency to diversify energy sources has never been greater.

Sources: Reuters, The Hindu BusinessLine, IANS, Outlook Business, CA Club India
